title: Alphabet, Pronunciation & German Phonetics
subtitle: Master the precise phonetic rules of standard High German (Hochdeutsch)

concept.title: The Phonetics of Hochdeutsch: Rules, Not Guesswork
concept.explanation:
Unlike English, German orthography is remarkably <rule>phonetic and consistent</rule>. Once you know the rules, you can pronounce any written German word correctly on sight.

### 1. The Core Alphabet & Special Characters
The German alphabet has 26 standard Latin letters, plus three **Umlauts** (<rule>ä</rule>, <rule>ö</rule>, <rule>ü</rule>) and the ligature **Eszett** (<rule>ß</rule>, called 'scharfes S').
- <rule>ä</rule> sounds like the 'e' in 'bed' (short: Männer) or like the 'ai' in 'air' (long: Bär).
- <rule>ö</rule> is produced by rounding your lips into an 'O' shape while saying English 'ay' (e.g., schön, hören).
- <rule>ü</rule> is produced by rounding your lips into an 'O' shape while saying English 'ee' (e.g., über, Tür).
- <rule>ß</rule> represents a sharp, voiceless 's' sound (like 'hiss') and is used strictly after long vowels and diphthongs (e.g., Straße, heiß).

### 2. The Golden Diphthong Rule: 'ei' vs. 'ie'
A classic trap for English speakers! Remember: **Pronounce the second letter!**
- <rule>ei</rule> is pronounced like English 'eye' or 'pie' (e.g., nein, mein, frei).
- <rule>ie</rule> is pronounced like English 'ee' or 'see' (e.g., Sie, hier, Liebe).
- <rule>eu</rule> / <rule>äu</rule> are both pronounced like English 'oy' in 'boy' (e.g., neu, Europa, Häuser).

### 3. Key Consonants & Clusters
- <rule>w</rule> is always pronounced like English 'V' (Wasser = 'Vah-ser').
- <rule>v</rule> in native German words sounds like English 'F' (Vater = 'Fah-ter', vier = 'feer'). In loan words it sounds like English 'V' (Vase, Visum).
- <rule>s</rule> before a vowel sounds like English 'Z' (Sonne = 'Zon-neh', sagen = 'Zah-gen'). Double 'ss' is always a sharp voiceless 's' (Wasser, dass).
- <rule>sp</rule> and <rule>st</rule> at the beginning of a syllable sound like 'shp' and 'sht' (Sport = 'Shport', Stadt = 'Shtadt').
- <rule>ch</rule> has two variants: the soft 'Ich-Laut' after front vowels e/i/ä/ö/ü (ich, nicht, Bücher) and the throaty 'Ach-Laut' after back vowels a/o/u (Bach, noch, Buch).

deepDives.title: Word-Final Devoicing (Auslautverhärtung)
deepDives.content: At the very end of a word or syllable, German voiced consonants (b, d, g) become devoiced into their unvoiced counterparts (p, t, k). For example: 'der Tag' is pronounced 'Tahk', 'das Bild' is pronounced 'Bilt', and 'das Grab' is pronounced 'Grahp'. When an ending is added (die Tage), the voiced 'g' returns!

deepDives.title: Never Pronounce 'Z' like English Zebra!
deepDives.content: In German, 'Z' is NEVER a buzzing sound. It is ALWAYS pronounced like 'TS' (as in the end of 'cats'). Say: Zeit ('Tsayt'), Zug ('Tsook'), zwei ('Tsvay'), Zimmer ('Tsim-mer'). Making a buzzing 'Z' immediately marks foreign speech.

guidedPractice.instruction: Which letter combination in German sounds like English 'eye'?
guidedPractice.prompt: Select the correct German diphthong that corresponds to the vowel sound in English 'pie' or 'eye':
guidedPractice.explanation: In German, 'ei' is always pronounced like English 'eye' (e.g. mein, nein, frei). In contrast, 'ie' is pronounced like English 'ee' (e.g. Sie, nie). Rule: pronounce the second letter!

guidedPractice.instruction: Identify the correct phonetic rule for German 'W' and 'V':
guidedPractice.prompt: How are the German letters 'W' (as in Wasser) and 'V' (as in Vater) pronounced?
guidedPractice.target: W is pronounced like English V; native V is pronounced like English F
options: W is pronounced like English W; V is pronounced like English V
W is pronounced like English V; native V is pronounced like English F
Both W and V are pronounced like English W
W is silent; V is always pronounced like B
guidedPractice.explanation: German 'W' is always a 'V' sound (Wasser = 'Vah-ser'). Native German 'V' is an 'F' sound (Vater = 'Fah-ter', vier = 'feer').

guidedPractice.instruction: Complete the word with the correct diphthong ('ei' or 'ie'):
guidedPractice.prompt: Ich trinke k___nen Kaffee. (meaning: I drink no coffee)
guidedPractice.explanation: The word is 'keinen' (from 'kein', meaning none/no), which is pronounced with the /aɪ/ sound, spelled 'ei'.

guidedPractice.instruction: Listen to the word and transcribe it accurately with its capitalization:
guidedPractice.explanation: 'Straße' (street) starts with 'St-' (pronounced 'Sht') and ends with an Eszett 'ß' after the long 'a' vowel.

guidedPractice.instruction: Arrange the words into the standard German greeting formula:
guidedPractice.prompt: Good day, my name is Schmidt.
guidedPractice.explanation: 'Guten Tag' introduces the greeting, followed by subject 'ich' and the conjugated verb 'heiße' in position 2.

readingPassage.title: Erste Schritte in Deutschland (First Steps in Germany)
readingPassage.germanText: Guten Tag! Mein Name ist Thomas Becker. Ich komme aus München. München ist eine sehr schöne Stadt in Bayern. Ich buchstabiere meinen Namen: T-H-O-M-A-S. Deutsch ist eine logische Sprache. Alle Substantive schreibt man groß.
readingPassage.englishSummary: Good day! My name is Thomas Becker. I come from Munich. Munich is a very beautiful city in Bavaria. I spell my name: T-H-O-M-A-S. German is a logical language. All nouns are capitalized.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where does Thomas come from?
comprehensionQuestions.explanation: The text states: 'Ich komme aus München.'

comprehensionQuestions.question: According to the passage, what orthographic rule applies to all German nouns?
comprehensionQuestions.explanation: The passage confirms: 'Alle Substantive schreibt man groß' (All nouns are capitalized).

listeningDialogue.title: Buchstabieren am Telefon (Spelling on the Phone)

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.text: Guten Morgen! Hier ist Weber. Wie heißen Sie bitte?
lines.translation: Good morning! This is Weber speaking. What is your name please?

lines.speaker: Herr Meier
lines.text: Guten Morgen Frau Weber. Mein Name ist Florian Meier.
lines.translation: Good morning Mrs. Weber. My name is Florian Meier.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.text: Wie schreibt man Meier? Mit e-i oder mit a-i?
lines.translation: How do you spell Meier? With e-i or with a-i?

lines.speaker: Herr Meier
lines.text: Mit M-E-I-E-R. Das ist die klassische Schreibweise.
lines.translation: With M-E-I-E-R. That is the classical spelling.

questions.question: Which diphthong is used to spell Herr Meier's surname?
questions.explanation: Herr Meier explicitly spells his name: 'Mit M-E-I-E-R'.

writing.prompt: Spell your full name in German and write three introductory words with German phonetic features (e.g. an umlaut word, an 'ei' word, and an 'sp/st' word).
guidelines: Use 'Guten Tag, mein Name ist...' to introduce yourself
Write out the spelling using German letter names (z.B. A-N-N-A)
Include at least one word with an umlaut (ä, ö, ü) or ß (z.B. schön, Straße, über)
writing.sampleResponse: Guten Tag! Mein Name ist David. Ich buchstabiere: D-A-V-I-D. Drei schöne deutsche Wörter sind: die Straße, das Wasser und das Buch.
selfCheckRubric: Did you capitalize all German nouns (z.B. Name, Straße, Wasser, Buch)?
Did you place the conjugated verb in Position 2 in declarative sentences?
Did you spell the Eszett (ß) correctly after long vowels?

speaking.prompt: Speak the following German phonetic test sentence clearly into the microphone:
speaking.targetSentence: Guten Tag, ich heiße David und komme aus Berlin.
speaking.translation: Good day, my name is David and I come from Berlin.
speaking.phoneticTips: Pronounce 'Guten Tag' with a crisp final 'k' sound, 'heiße' with a clear /aɪ/ diphthong, and 'Berlin' with emphasis on the second syllable.

questions.instruction: Test 1: Identify the correct pronunciation of German 'Z':
questions.prompt: How is the German letter 'Z' in 'Zeit' or 'Zug' pronounced?
questions.explanation: German 'Z' is always pronounced like 'ts' in 'cats', never like 'z' in 'zebra'.

questions.instruction: Test 2: Which word contains the vowel sound /iː/ (English 'ee')?
questions.prompt: Select the word pronounced with the long /iː/ sound:
questions.explanation: 'Liebe' contains 'ie', which is pronounced /iː/. The words 'mein', 'kein', and 'nein' contain 'ei', pronounced /aɪ/.

questions.instruction: Test 3: Fill in the missing ligature:
questions.explanation: 'Straße' is spelled with 'ß' because it follows a long 'a' vowel.

questions.instruction: Test 4: What is the sound of 'sp' and 'st' at the beginning of a German word?
questions.prompt: How do native speakers pronounce words like 'Sport' and 'Stadt'?
questions.explanation: At the start of a syllable, 'sp' and 'st' are pronounced 'shp' and 'sht' in German.

questions.instruction: Test 5: Reorder the sentence into standard German syntax:
questions.prompt: My name is Julia and I come from Germany.
questions.target: Mein Name ist Julia und ich komme aus Deutschland.
questions.explanation: The sentence links two main clauses with coordinating conjunction 'und' in Position 0.
